extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students/scholars of sociology, political history, and anthropology
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate social, political, economic, and moral traits that distinguish the 'industrial' type of society (characterized by voluntary cooperation and exchange) from the 'militant' type (characterized by compulsory cooperation and war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑coercive local government — council-based dispute resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Indigenous or village government exercised by an informally approved council or committee where 'the committee assemble and discuss the affairs of the village and its inhabitants. All petty disputes, both of a civil and criminal nature, are settled there.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Santals, Lepchas, Jakuns, Arafuras — presence of patriarchs who rarely interfere; locally chosen heads; arbitration rather than violent enforcement. Anti-pattern: strong centralized coercive rule or hereditary chieftainship that routinely imposes will by force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence or faintness of class distinctions / status relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Class distinctions do not exist or are only faintly indicated; the relation of status is absent so that individuals are not rigidly subordinated by rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen in unwarlike tribes and societies where social life is not organized around compulsory military obligations. Contrast with militant societies exhibiting rigid status systems (slaves, serfs, vassals, nobles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing principle: voluntary cooperation rather than compulsory cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial type organizes social activities around voluntary cooperation (exchange under agreement), contrasting with the militant type's organizing principle of compulsory cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key diagnostic: growth of institutions exhibiting voluntary cooperation as militant institutions decline. Implication: greater freedom of movement, association, and contract. Anti-pattern: institutions that require constant enforced subordination for collective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of contract replaces system of status
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts and agreed exchanges supplant hereditary or ascribed status relations (servile labor-services, vassal obligations), so personal relations are governed by agreement rather than enforced rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical markers: commutation of labor-services for money, mitigation of villanage and serfdom, enfranchisement moving people from subject to governing classes. Contrast: places where status remains dominant (e.g., many Continental areas historically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decreased regulation of personal life and freedoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminished restraints over individual actions: people less tied to localities, freer in religion, political expression, dress, forming private combinations, and holding meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: abolition of laws forbidding artisans to travel, lifting of restrictions on trade unions, expanded freedom of the press and public meetings. Anti-pattern: regimes dictating religion, dress, and everyday practices (e.g., heavy policing of personal behaviors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased public protection and administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: State protection of persons and property increases; one chief function of rulers and agents is to administer justice rather than to appropriate individuals to the state's ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifestations: improved police systems, county courts, provisions to prevent selling/delaying/denying justice. Anti-pattern: state that takes property/labor extensively while failing to protect citizens from crime and internal violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decline in warfare as dominant social activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Wars become less frequent and less the business of all freemen; external hostilities are occasional and internal perpetual wars decline, permitting industrial life to grow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative marker: societies where war consolidations historically inhibited industrial development (e.g., medieval continental areas) vs. societies where relative internal peace allowed industrial growth (e.g., England in certain periods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic reorientation: working population produces for its own benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively large population engages in production and distribution for its own benefit rather than existing predominantly to support the fighting part of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator of industrial type: development of production/distribution institutions oriented to civilian welfare; the fighting part exists mainly to protect the working part. Anti-pattern: economies organized primarily to sustain military elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government as product and form of industrial growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Rise of representative (parliamentary) government accompanies and is produced by industrial development and is characteristic of the industrial type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evidence: growth of popular power (e.g., House of Commons) coinciding with industrial growth; absence or abortion of representative assemblies where militancy persisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation of arbitrary exactions and chronic fiscal oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Decrease of arbitrary tallages, confiscations, and exactions by rulers; fewer seizures of property and less repeated reselling of municipal privileges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen historically where contract and protection expand; contrasted with militant regimes where monarchs acted as "universal proprietor," imposing heavy burdens and conscripting labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction and reform of punitive/legal severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Penal code amelioration: reduction of capital offenses, abolition of degrading punishments (pillory, debt imprisonment), and general trend toward less severe state punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical trend in industrializing states: abolition of public whipping of females, gradual reduction of capital offenses to very few, and other penal reforms. Anti-pattern: expansion of capital crimes and draconian punishments during militant periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less intrusive regulation of industry and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial type features diminished micro-regulation of manufacturers and agricultural producers (fewer destructive regulations of devices, fewer restrictions on crops, imports, and market sales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: France (historically heavy supervision of industry and commerce) vs. England (progress toward allowing joint-stock banks, freer trade, fewer import restrictions). Anti-pattern: state agents destroying improvements or penalizing inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition from compulsory military service to voluntary enlistment
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement away from conscription and press-gangs toward voluntary military service, reducing the state's direct claim on citizens' lives and liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sign of post-war revival toward industrial traits; accompanies other expansions of personal freedom and reduction of coercive state power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal character traits: strong sense of individual freedom and pride
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of industrial/unwarlike societies display a strong sense of personal freedom and determination to maintain it (e.g., flee the country rather than submit to coercion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnographic examples: Bodo, Dhimals, Lepchas, Jakuns who resist oppression and show pride in autonomy. Anti-pattern: socialization into obedience and cringing required by militant structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal character traits: respect for others and rarity of interpersonal violence
rubrics_metrics.description: High respect for others' claims, rarity of personal collisions or violent quarrels, absence of lex talionis and blood-revenge norms; disputes commonly settled by arbitration or mutual amends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lepchas 'rarely quarrel,' Jakuns settle disputes 'without fighting or malice,' Arafuras live 'in peace and brotherly love.' Anti-pattern: cultures endorsing blood-revenge and frequent interpersonal vengeance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal character traits: honesty, low crime, and humane sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities exhibit scrupulous honesty, low incidence of crime (theft, serious offenses), forgiving attitudes, mutual amends, beneficence, and a tendency to use wealth to assist neighbors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited testimonies: 'crime of a serious nature is unknown among them,' 'never known to steal anything' (Jakuns), and examples of paying debts of poorer villagers to settle differences. Use as evidence for industrial-type social morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic diagnostic: predominance of exchange of services under agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential test: social activities are predominantly characterized by exchange of services under agreement (i.e., market/contract relations) rather than enforced obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's concluding diagnostic: observe decline of institutions of militancy and concurrent growth of institutions of exchange/contract to infer industrial type. This is the overarching criterion synthesizing political, economic, and moral traits.
